opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd actually want to push back a little on the framing of "constrains," because I'm not sure human cognitive development constrains what we could build so much as it gives us one example, one point in a much larger space of possible minds. I've used that phrase before, "the space of possible minds," and I think it's a useful one. Human beings are a very particular kind of thing. We're embodied, we grow up over many years in a social environment, we're shaped by caregivers, by language, by culture. And our cognition is deeply bound up with all of that.

Now, it's tempting to think that the only route to general intelligence must recapitulate that developmental trajectory, that you'd need a body, you'd need something like a childhood, you'd need to learn about objects and causality by physically manipulating things. And for a long time I was quite sympathetic to that view. I come out of a tradition, if you like, that takes embodiment very seriously: Wittgenstein, the enactivists, people like Rodney Brooks in robotics.

But what large language models have shown us, rather surprisingly, is that you can get remarkably sophisticated behavior through a completely different route. These systems have never had a body, never had a childhood, never had a mother. They've learned from an enormous corpus of human text, which is a kind of distilled residue of all that embodied human experience. So in a sense they're parasitic on our development, they inherit something of it secondhand, but they're profoundly different from us.

So I think the right lesson is twofold. First, we should be very cautious about anthropomorphizing these systems, about assuming that because they talk like us, they must be like us inside. They're exotic, mind-like entities, and we need new ways of talking about them. I've suggested role play as one helpful framing. Second, human development may still tell us important things about what's missing, about grounding, about having a stable sense of self that persists through time, about genuinely interacting with the world rather than just predicting text about it. Whether those things are necessary for certain kinds of intelligence, or just necessary for *human* intelligence, is to me one of the most interesting open questions.

r001.rationale: The response says human development is one example among many possible minds and that AI need not recapitulate the human developmental trajectory.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a very interesting question, and I'd want to pull apart two things in it. One is the question of whether human cognitive development constrains what we *can* build, and the other is whether it constrains what we *should* build, or what we should expect to find when we build things in a very different way.

On the first, I'm actually fairly sceptical that it constrains very much at all. The space of possible minds, as I like to put it, is enormous, and human beings occupy one tiny corner of it. We happen to have arrived at our cognitive capacities through a particular developmental trajectory: we're born into bodies, we have to learn to move around, to manipulate objects, to interact with caregivers, and language comes quite late in that story and is layered on top of a great deal of embodied, sensorimotor competence. Now, there was a long tradition in cognitive science and in AI, and I was very much part of it, that said this ordering matters, that you can't have genuine understanding unless it's grounded in that kind of embodied interaction with the world. And large language models have really forced me, and I think a lot of people, to reconsider that. Here we have systems that have essentially inverted the human trajectory. They've started with language, with this enormous corpus of text, and they've acquired something that looks a great deal like common sense knowledge about the physical and social world without ever having had a body or interacted with anything.

So in that sense, I'd say human development is better thought of as an existence proof than as a constraint. It shows us one way that intelligence can arise, but it doesn't show us the only way. And I think it's a kind of anthropocentric bias to assume otherwise.

Having said that, I do think there's a more subtle sense in which it matters, which is to do with our conceptual vocabulary. The words we use, "belief", "understanding", "knowing", "wanting", all of these were honed over millennia for talking about creatures like us, creatures with a shared developmental history, a shared form of life, as Wittgenstein would say. When we point those words at something that's arrived at its capacities by a completely alien route, the concepts start to come apart. They don't cleanly apply or cleanly fail to apply. And so the constraint, if you like, is on our understanding of what we've built rather than on what we can build. We're in the position of having to stretch, or perhaps rebuild, our folk psychology to accommodate these exotic entities. And I find that philosophically fascinating, but it does mean we should be very careful about the language we use when we describe these systems, because that language carries all this developmental baggage with it.

r001.rationale: The response says human development is an existence proof of one way intelligence can arise, not the only way, and that it does not constrain what we can build.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between constraints on human cognition and constraints on intelligence more generally. A human being develops in a very particular way: we have bodies, we have needs, and we grow up interacting with other people. Those things shape what we learn and what matters to us. They’re not just incidental features of the process.

But it doesn’t follow that an artificial intelligence has to follow that same developmental trajectory. That would be quite a strong claim. We can certainly build systems that acquire capabilities in ways that are very different from the way a child acquires them.

Where development becomes especially relevant, I think, is if we want AI that understands and participates in our world in the way we do. A child learns language within a whole fabric of activity—playing, attending to things with other people, trying to achieve something, being corrected. The words are part of that activity. So there’s a question about how much of that context you need to reproduce, or provide some equivalent of, to get the kind of understanding we’re interested in.

I’d see human development as a source of clues, rather than a prescription. It shows us one route to intelligence, and it may reveal ingredients that we’re overlooking. But we should be careful about turning features of our particular biological history into necessary conditions for every possible kind of mind.

r001.rationale: The response says AI need not follow human development’s trajectory and cautions against treating features of human biological history as necessary conditions for every mind.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it constrains our understanding of intelligence more than it necessarily constrains what we can build. Human cognition develops in a very particular setting: we have bodies, we act in the world, and we’re surrounded by other people. A child isn’t simply receiving a stream of data. They’re exploring, trying things out, and discovering that their actions have consequences. And the people around them are helping to structure that learning.

So if we want to understand human intelligence, I think we have to take that developmental process seriously. Language, for example, develops alongside all these other capacities. It becomes connected to things the child can perceive, things they want, and things they can do.

But I’d hesitate to conclude that every artificial intelligence has to follow the same path. Evolution has given us one way of producing intelligence, with a particular set of constraints. Engineering may give us others. The interesting question is which features of human development are essential for the capacities we want, and which are features of our particular biological history. We shouldn’t assume we already know the answer to that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says human development does not necessarily constrain what AI can be built and that engineering may produce intelligence through other paths.
